hints: Notice the wording using only the definition of acceleration - start from what acceleration $a$ means as change of velocity $v-u$ over time $t$.
Write the definition for uniform acceleration as $a = \frac{v-u}{t}$ and check which listed equation uses only $v$, $u$, $a$ and $t$ with no displacement $s$.
Rearrange $a = \frac{v-u}{t}$ to make final velocity $v$ the subject and match the result against the four equations.
walkthrough: Recall the definition of acceleration for straight-line motion: rate of change of velocity, so $a = \frac{\text{change in velocity}}{\text{time taken}}$.
For initial velocity $u$, final velocity $v$ and time $t$ with uniform $a$, this is $a = \frac{v-u}{t}$.
Multiply both sides by $t$ to give $at = v - u$.
Add $u$ to both sides to make $v$ the subject: $v = u + at$. No displacement $s$ or average velocity was needed.
The other equations all contain $s$ and require the definition of displacement or average velocity as well. This is option C.

A.explanation: This needs displacement $s$ and also the idea of average velocity or area under a velocity-time graph, not acceleration alone.

B.explanation: This uses average velocity $\frac{(u+v)}{2}$ multiplied by $t$ to get $s$, so it needs the definition of velocity as well as acceleration.

C.explanation: This is a direct rearrangement of the definition $a = \frac{v-u}{t}$ to $v = u + at$, using no displacement $s$.

D.explanation: This eliminates $t$ to link $v$, $u$, $a$ and $s$, so it must combine the acceleration definition with the displacement equation.
